\chapter{More Than One}
\label{ch:bn-more-than-one}
\hlchaptermodality{33}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can sort a noun into living or not, put the plural its group demands on it, and stand an adjective in front of it.}

One question about a noun — is it alive? — chooses between two plural endings, and every noun the book owns goes through the one its group demands. The adjective rule that thirty-two chapters used without stating is stated.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[jīb ār jinish]{\bn{জীব} \bn{আর} \bn{জিনিস} (jīb ār jinish) — alive, and not}

\label{lesson:BN-C22-animacy}



\begin{quote}
Ask \textbf{what is this?} Then say \textbf{this shirt}, with both ends.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} two chapters back, the ending that turns a noun into \emph{the} one — \emph{-ṭā}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the split}
Every noun you have learned belongs to one of two groups, and Bengali has been waiting to be told which:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{group} & \textbf{what is in it} & \textbf{examples from this book} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\bn{জীব}} — living & people and animals & \textbf{\bn{ভাই}}, \textbf{\bn{বোন}}, \textbf{\bn{বন্ধু}} \\
\textbf{\bn{জিনিস}} — thing & everything else & \textbf{\bn{জামা}}, \textbf{\bn{চা}}, \textbf{\bn{জল}}, \textbf{\bn{নাক}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

This is not decoration. It decides two things that are about to matter:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{which ending makes it plural} — the next two lessons
  \item \textbf{which classifier counts it} — you have met one of them already
\end{itemize}

Spanish makes the same kind of demand and answers it with gender, which has to be learned word by word because a table has no visible femininity. Bengali's question — \emph{is it alive?} — can be answered by looking.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the borderline, and what to do about it}]
Two warnings, and they are the whole difficulty:

\textbf{Body parts are things.} \textbf{\bn{নাক}} and \textbf{\bn{মুখ}} belong to a living person and are themselves \textbf{\bn{জিনিস}}. The test is whether the noun names something alive, not whether it belongs to something alive.

\textbf{Respect can move a noun up.} A person spoken of warmly takes the living endings even when a plain speaker might not bother. That is the same warmth \textbf{\bn{টি}} carries, and it runs right through Bengali grammar.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item which group — \emph{bhāi}, \emph{bôn}, \emph{bôndhu}
  \item which group — \emph{jāmā}, \emph{chā}, \emph{jôl}, \emph{nāk}
  \item the two group names — \emph{jīb}, \emph{jinish}
  \item the tricky one, and why — \emph{nāk} is \textbf{\bn{জিনিস}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What question does Bengali ask about a noun that Spanish answers with gender? (\textbf{Is it alive?}) Which group does \textbf{\bn{নাক}} belong to, and why? (\textbf{\bn{জিনিস}} — the test is what the noun names, not what it is attached to.) And what two things does the answer decide? (\textbf{The plural ending}, and \textbf{the classifier}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-rā]{\bn{রা} (-rā) — more than one, and alive}

\label{lesson:BN-C22-ra}



\begin{quote}
Which group is \textbf{\bn{ভাই}} in, and which is \textbf{\bn{জামা}} in?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{রা}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{ভাই}} — \emph{bhāi} — brother.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{ভাইরা}} — \emph{bhāirā} — \textbf{brothers.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{বন্ধু}} — \emph{bôndhu} — friend.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{বন্ধুরা}} — \emph{bôndhurā} — \textbf{friends.}
\end{quote}

Twenty chapters of family and friends, and every one of them has been strictly one person. \textbf{\bn{রা}} on the end makes them many — and it is allowed \textbf{only} on the living group. Put it on a shirt and a Bengali speaker will stop you.

When the noun ends in a consonant, an \textbf{\bn{এ}} appears to carry the ending:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{বোন}} — \emph{bôn} — sister.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{বোনেরা}} — \emph{bônerā} — \textbf{sisters.}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: Bengali does not insist}]
English forces the choice on every noun in every sentence: it is \emph{brother} or \emph{brothers}, never neutral. Bengali does not. A bare \textbf{\bn{ভাই}} is happy to mean one brother or several, and the ending goes on only when the plurality is the point.

That is why the ending has felt absent from this book: it has not been hiding. Bengali has not needed it yet.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bhāi}, then \emph{bhāirā}
  \item \emph{bôndhu}, then \emph{bôndhurā}
  \item the one that needs the extra vowel — \emph{bôn}, then \emph{bônerā}
  \item pointing at them — \emph{ei bhāirā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which group of nouns may take \textbf{\bn{রা}}? (\textbf{The living one.}) What appears before it after a consonant? (\textbf{\bn{এ}}.) And must a Bengali noun be marked plural whenever it is plural? (\textbf{No} — only when it matters.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-gulo]{\bn{গুলো} (-gulo) — more than one, and not alive}

\label{lesson:BN-C22-gulo}



\begin{quote}
Make \textbf{\bn{ভাই}} plural. Then try the same ending on \textbf{\bn{জামা}} and say why it is wrong.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{গুলো}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{জামাগুলো}} — \emph{jāmāgulo} — \textbf{the shirts.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{চোখগুলো}} — \emph{chokhgulo} — \textbf{the eyes.}
\end{quote}

The \textbf{\bn{জিনিস}} half of the split gets its own ending, and it is a longer one. Where \textbf{\bn{রা}} only pluralises, \textbf{\bn{গুলো}} pluralises \textbf{and} definitises: it means \emph{the} shirts, the particular ones, not shirts in general.

So this ending is doing the classifier's job as well as the plural's — which is exactly what you should expect from a language whose singular \emph{the} is also a stuck-on piece.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the full table, finally}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{group and noun} & \textbf{one, definite} & \textbf{more than one} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\bn{জীব}} — \textbf{\bn{ভাই}} & \bn{ভাইটি} & \textbf{\bn{ভাইরা}} \\
\textbf{\bn{জিনিস}} — \textbf{\bn{জামা}} & \bn{জামাটা} & \textbf{\bn{জামাগুলো}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read the last column and the split earns itself. Two endings, chosen by one question you can answer by looking, and the whole of Bengali's number system for an A1 learner is in that table.

There is a careful twin here too — \textbf{\bn{গুলি}}, standing to \textbf{\bn{গুলো}} as \textbf{\bn{টি}} stands to \textbf{\bn{টা}}. Recognise it; say \textbf{\bn{গুলো}}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{jāmāgulo} — the shirts
  \item the two halves back to back — \emph{bhāirā}, \emph{jāmāgulo}
  \item pointing — \emph{ei jāmāgulo}, \emph{oi jāmāgulo}
  \item with a colour in front — \emph{lāl jāmāgulo}
  \item the pair of eyes — \emph{chokhgulo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which group takes \textbf{\bn{গুলো}}? (\textbf{\bn{জিনিস}} — the not-living one.) What does it add beyond plurality? (\textbf{Definiteness} — \emph{the} shirts.) And what is the careful form? (\textbf{\bn{গুলি}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[lāl jāmā]{\bn{লাল} \bn{জামা} (lāl jāmā) — a red shirt}

\label{lesson:BN-C22-adj-order}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{the shirts}. Then say \textbf{red}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: where the adjective goes}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{লাল} \bn{জামা}} — \emph{lāl jāmā} — \textbf{a red shirt.}
\end{quote}

Chapter twenty-six gave you five colours and used every one of them as a sentence on its own — \emph{the shirt is red}. Not once did a colour stand \textbf{in front of} a noun, which is where an adjective actually lives most of the time.

It goes \textbf{in front}, and — this is the part worth keeping — it \textbf{never changes}. Not for the group the noun is in, not for how many there are, not for anything:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\bn{লাল} \bn{জামা}} — a red shirt
  \item \textbf{\bn{লাল} \bn{জামাগুলো}} — the red shirts
  \item \textbf{\bn{লাল} \bn{জামাটা}} — the red shirt
\end{itemize}

One form of \textbf{\bn{লাল}}, three phrases. Spanish would have made you write \emph{rojo}, \emph{rojos} and \emph{roja}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the queue, filled in}]
Chapter thirty-two laid out a queue and left a slot empty. This is the word that fills it:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{slot} & \textbf{what goes there} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
first & pointer & \textbf{\bn{এই}} \\
second & number & \textbf{\bn{একটা}} \\
third & \textbf{adjective} & \textbf{\bn{লাল}} \\
last & noun + ending & \textbf{\bn{জামা}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

And \textbf{\bn{ভালো}}, which you have had since chapter three as \emph{well} and as \emph{good}, is an adjective like any other and takes the same slot: \textbf{\bn{ভালো} \bn{বন্ধু}} — a good friend.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{lāl jāmā} — a red shirt
  \item all five colours in front of the same noun — \emph{lāl}, \emph{kālo}, \emph{nīl}, \emph{shādā}, \emph{shôbuj jāmā}
  \item unchanged across number — \emph{lāl jāmā}, \emph{lāl jāmāgulo}
  \item the whole queue — \emph{ei ekṭā lāl jāmā}
  \item \emph{bhālo bôndhu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which side of the noun does a Bengali adjective sit on? (\textbf{In front}.) Does it change for number or for the noun's group? (\textbf{No} — never.) And which slot of the queue is it? (\textbf{The third}, between the number and the noun.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-rā · -gulo · lāl jāmā]{More than one}

\label{lesson:BN-R22-more-than-one}



\begin{quote}
One question decides which of two endings a noun takes. What is the question, and what are the two endings?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{bhāirā}, \emph{bônerā}, \emph{bôndhurā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{jāmāgulo}, \emph{chokhgulo}
  \item \emph{Say it:} unchanged in front — \emph{lāl jāmā}, \emph{lāl jāmāgulo}
  \item \emph{Recall:} two chapters back, the ending that makes a noun \emph{the} one — \emph{-ṭā}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: the distant band — the whole book, in the plural}
Sort every noun this book owns into its group, then pluralise it the way its group demands. Cold, from memory.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the living ones — \emph{bhāirā}, \emph{bônerā}, \emph{bôndhurā}
  \item the things — \emph{jāmāgulo}, \emph{kāpôṛgulo}, \emph{chokhgulo}, \emph{nākgulo}
  \item the two that catch people out, and why — \emph{nāk} and \emph{hridôy} are \textbf{\bn{জিনিস}}
  \item the food, definite and plural — \emph{bhātgulo}, \emph{chāgulo}
  \item with a colour and a pointer — \emph{ei lāl jāmāgulo}, \emph{oi kālo kāpôṛgulo}
  \item one, another, then all of them — \emph{ekṭā jāmā}, \emph{ārekṭā jāmā}, \emph{jāmāgulo}
  \item the family, singular and plural — \emph{pôribārṭā}, then \emph{bhāirā}
  \item asking about a pile of them — \emph{eṭā ki?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which ending does a living noun take, and which does a thing take? (\textbf{\bn{রা}} and \textbf{\bn{গুলো}}.) Which of the two also means \emph{the}? (\textbf{\bn{গুলো}}.) Where does an adjective stand, and does it change? (\textbf{In front}, and \textbf{no}.) And which letter, three lessons before this chapter, made all of it writable? (\textbf{\bn{ট}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
